traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
title: Sepsis & Septic Shock: Recognition, Resuscitation and Source Control
html:
Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection. Septic shock is the higher-risk subset in which profound circulatory and cellular or metabolic abnormalities persist despite initial resuscitation. The RN must recognize change before collapse, activate the sepsis pathway, support time-sensitive diagnostics and antimicrobials, reassess every intervention, identify harmful fluid accumulation, and help secure definitive source control. A normal temperature, normal blood pressure, or single reassuring laboratory value does not exclude sepsis.

Learning goals

  • Distinguish uncomplicated infection, sepsis, and septic shock using organ dysfunction and perfusion—not fever alone.
  • Recognize early and late cues in older, immunocompromised, pregnant, postoperative, and otherwise high-risk adults.
  • Coordinate cultures, lactate, antimicrobials, fluids, vasopressors, and source control without avoidable delay.
  • Use dynamic assessment, serial lactate, capillary refill, urine output, mentation, skin and respiratory findings to evaluate perfusion.
  • Prevent medication, vascular-access, fluid-overload, pressure-injury, glucose, thrombosis, delirium, and transition-of-care harm.

Sepsis is infection plus dangerous organ dysfunction

Look for a suspected or confirmed infection together with a new departure from baseline: altered mentation, increasing oxygen need, tachypnea, hypotension, oliguria, mottling or prolonged capillary refill, rising lactate, thrombocytopenia, bilirubin or creatinine elevation, coagulopathy, or other organ failure. Tachycardia, fever, hypothermia, leukocytosis, leukopenia, chills, weakness, hyperglycemia, or hypoglycemia may support concern but are not diagnostic by themselves.

Older adults may present with confusion, weakness, a fall, poor intake, or functional decline. Immunocompromised patients may not mount fever or leukocytosis. Beta blockers may blunt tachycardia. Pregnancy changes normal heart rate, respiratory rate, blood volume, and laboratory values and requires an obstetric pathway. Always compare with the patient's baseline and ask, “Could infection be causing this new organ dysfunction?”

Screening supports judgment—it does not replace it

The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends NEWS/NEWS2, MEWS, or SIRS over qSOFA as a single hospital screening tool. No score, biomarker, or test independently rules sepsis in or out. Screening should trigger a clinician assessment, not an automatic diagnosis or a reason to dismiss concern below a threshold.

qSOFA findings—altered mentation, respiratory rate at least 22/min, and systolic pressure at or below 100 mm Hg—can identify increased risk, but waiting for two findings may miss earlier disease. SOFA describes organ dysfunction in respiratory, coagulation, liver, cardiovascular, neurologic, and renal systems; it is not a bedside permission slip to delay treatment. Record the precise change, time, suspected source, and trajectory.

Septic shock is more than one low pressure

The Sepsis-3 clinical construct identifies septic shock when sepsis requires vasopressors to maintain mean arterial pressure (MAP) at least 65 mm Hg and lactate remains above 2 mmol/L after adequate volume resuscitation. This construct describes a high-risk population, but emergency treatment begins before every criterion is fulfilled. A patient with rapidly falling pressure, altered mentation, mottled or ashen skin, cyanosis, severe tachycardia, or escalating oxygen need may have unstable shock and needs immediate resuscitation.

Lactate is a risk and perfusion marker, not a direct meter of infection severity or a command to give unlimited fluid. It may rise with adrenergic stress, seizures, liver dysfunction, medications, or impaired clearance. Trend lactate with the examination, capillary refill, urine output, mentation, hemodynamics, oxygenation, and response to treatment. Do not keep giving fluid solely until lactate normalizes.

First response: stabilize, identify, and communicate

Activate the local sepsis or rapid-response pathway. Assess airway protection, work of breathing, oxygenation, circulation, mental status, skin perfusion, temperature, pain, urine output, and glucose. Obtain frequent vital signs and establish appropriate vascular access. Identify possible sources—lung, urinary tract, abdomen, skin or soft tissue, vascular device, wound, central nervous system, bone or joint, or reproductive tract—and ask about recent procedures, implants, travel, antibiotics, resistant organisms, immunosuppression, allergies, pregnancy, and goals of care.

Communicate a concise time-stamped picture: suspected source, new organ dysfunction, blood pressure and MAP trend, respiratory support, mental status, urine output, lactate, cultures, antimicrobial allergy, fluid given and response, and current vasoactive support. “Possible sepsis” is more actionable when paired with the exact cues and trajectory.

Cultures and antimicrobials must be coordinated

Collect blood cultures as soon as possible and ideally before antimicrobials, plus source-specific specimens of adequate quality. Do not allow difficult cultures, urine collection, imaging, or transfer to create a dangerous delay in treatment. Label specimens accurately and record whether they were obtained before or after the first antimicrobial dose.

For possible, probable, or definite septic shock, and for probable or definite sepsis without shock, the 2026 guideline recommends immediate antimicrobial therapy, ideally within one hour of recognition. For possible sepsis without shock, rapidly assess infectious versus noninfectious causes; if concern persists, give antimicrobials within three hours of first suspicion. A low likelihood of infection without shock may justify close monitoring while treatment is deferred by the qualified team.

Verify allergy phenotype, prior cultures and resistant organisms, infection source, kidney and liver function, weight, pregnancy, interactions, and recent antimicrobial exposure. Administer the authorized loading dose on time. Later, support daily review, susceptibility-guided narrowing, dose optimization, toxicity monitoring, and shortest effective duration after adequate source control. Stewardship means correct early coverage followed by deliberate reassessment—not undertreatment of shock.

Initial fluid requires repeated reassessment

For sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock, the 2026 guideline suggests at least 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid during the first three hours, with volume individualized to patient characteristics and context. Use actual body weight, or adjusted or ideal weight when BMI exceeds 30 kg/m², according to the guideline and local protocol. Crystalloid is preferred; starch solutions should not be used. Do not interpret a suggested initial volume as an order to infuse without assessment.

Before, during, and after each bolus, reassess MAP and pulse pressure, heart rate, capillary refill, skin and mentation, lung sounds and oxygen need, jugular venous findings when useful, urine output, edema, weight and cumulative balance. Dynamic response to a passive leg raise or small fluid challenge measured through stroke volume or pulse-pressure change is more informative than a static pressure alone. Heart failure, kidney disease, cirrhosis, pulmonary hypertension, and pregnancy require particularly close titration—but do not justify leaving shock untreated.

Stop automatic fluid escalation when perfusion fails to improve or signs of congestion appear. New crackles, rising oxygen or ventilator requirement, worsening edema, elevated venous pressure, abdominal hypertension, or poor fluid responsiveness may signal harm. Escalate for vasopressor and hemodynamic review rather than repeatedly treating every low pressure with another bolus.

Vasopressors restore pressure while the cause is treated

For septic shock, norepinephrine is the usual first-line vasopressor. The initial MAP target for most adults is about 65 mm Hg; the 2026 guideline suggests an initial range of 60–65 mm Hg for adults age 65 or older rather than routinely targeting higher values. Targets are individualized for chronic hypertension, neurologic or cardiovascular disease, pregnancy, perfusion findings, and treatment response.

Do not delay a needed vasopressor solely while waiting for central access. A peripheral infusion may be started through the local protocol with a well-functioning, visible vein and frequent site and distal-perfusion checks while definitive access is arranged. Trace every line to the pump, verify concentration and titration orders, use the designated lumen, monitor rhythm and pressure continuously as required, and watch for infiltration, extravasation, ischemia, dysrhythmia, or an abrupt empty bag. Follow the emergency protocol for suspected extravasation.

In profoundly unstable shock, the 2026 guideline allows case-by-case concurrent vasopressor initiation with crystalloid rather than waiting for an entire fluid sequence. Persistent shock may require additional vasopressor, inotrope, corticosteroid, or mechanical support decisions based on cardiac function and hemodynamics. The RN does not select these independently but must identify nonresponse and toxicity quickly.

Source control is definitive treatment

Antimicrobials cannot drain an abscess, relieve an infected obstruction, debride necrotic tissue, repair a perforation, or remove an infected device. Rapidly evaluate for an anatomic source needing intervention. When source control is required, the 2026 guideline suggests early treatment, ideally within six hours of the sepsis or septic-shock diagnosis.

Prepare for drainage, surgery, endoscopy, urologic decompression, wound debridement, or device removal as indicated. Maintain fasting status when ordered without withholding resuscitation, correct severe coagulopathy and instability as directed, ensure replacement access before removing a necessary infected intravascular catheter, and obtain cultures from the controlled source. After intervention, reassess perfusion, pain, output, bleeding, organ function, and antimicrobial plan.

Track every organ and prevent secondary harm

Trend oxygenation and ventilation, consciousness and delirium, MAP and peripheral perfusion, rhythm, urine output and kidney function, liver tests, platelets and coagulation, glucose, lactate, temperature, skin, mobility, nutrition, and cumulative fluid balance. Escalating oxygen need, oliguria, worsening confusion, thrombocytopenia, rising bilirubin or creatinine, ileus, cool or mottled extremities, or new bleeding may indicate evolving multiorgan dysfunction.

Use lung-protective ventilation and prone-position pathways when ARDS criteria are met; administer pharmacologic venous-thromboembolism prophylaxis unless contraindicated; start enteral nutrition when appropriate; prevent pressure injury and device infection; and use delirium, pain, sedation, sleep, mobility, and restraint-minimization strategies. Begin insulin therapy at the ordered threshold—current guidance recommends starting at glucose at or above 180 mg/dL rather than pursuing tight normal glucose that increases hypoglycemia.

Recovery continues after survival

Sepsis survivors may experience weakness, neuropathy, cognitive change, sleep disturbance, anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress, chronic organ dysfunction, medication changes, and recurrent infection risk. Involve patients and support persons in goals and updates. Reconcile medicines, lines and wounds, mobility and nutrition needs, follow-up laboratories, rehabilitation, mental-health support, and signs requiring urgent reassessment. Explain the infection and source-control plan in plain language.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify suspected infection, new organ dysfunction, perfusion and respiratory trends, high-risk conditions, recent procedures or devices, and the patient's baseline.
  2. Analyze cues: Compare sepsis with hemorrhage, cardiogenic or obstructive shock, medication effect, adrenal crisis, anaphylaxis, and other mimics; one patient can have more than one shock mechanism.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Threatened airway, severe hypoxemia, rapidly worsening shock, altered consciousness, oliguria, mottling, and an uncontrolled source require immediate escalation.
  4. Generate solutions: Plan cultures without treatment delay, appropriate antimicrobials, individualized crystalloid, vasopressor support, dynamic perfusion checks, imaging, and source control.
  5. Take action: Activate the pathway, administer authorized treatment on time, monitor vascular access and every organ, communicate response after each intervention, and prevent secondary harm.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Look for improving mentation, capillary refill, MAP, urine output, oxygenation, lactate trend, source control and organ function without fluid overload or medication toxicity.

Clinical example

An older adult with an obstructed infected ureter develops confusion, tachypnea, MAP 55 mm Hg, mottled knees, oliguria, and lactate 4.1 mmol/L. The RN activates the sepsis pathway, supports oxygenation, obtains cultures without delaying immediate authorized antimicrobials, begins ordered crystalloid with frequent lung and perfusion reassessment, and prepares peripheral norepinephrine under protocol when hypotension persists. The RN reports response to each intervention and helps expedite urgent urinary decompression. A temporary blood-pressure improvement does not cancel the need for source control.

Original educational synthesis aligned with the 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign. Screening, antimicrobial selection and timing, fluid volume, hemodynamic targets, vascular access, vasoactive therapy, source control, organ support, and discharge care require current patient data, authorized orders, local protocols, and qualified critical-care, infectious-disease, surgical, obstetric, or other specialist input. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, continuing education, certification, or an official SCCM, ESICM, JAMA, or CDC product.
